title: Adult sepsis and septic shock (India)

symptoms: Fever or feeling abnormally cold; rigors and profound malaise.
Breathlessness, confusion or reduced urine; ask about respiratory, urinary, abdominal, skin and device symptoms.
physicalSigns: Hypotension, tachypnoea, altered mentation, mottling or delayed capillary refill; fever may be absent.
Examine the chest, abdomen, skin, joints and indwelling devices for a source.
redFlags: Persistent hypotension, increasing oxygen requirement, reduced consciousness or progressive organ dysfunction: request critical care immediately.
Septic shock criteria: vasopressors needed to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) at least 65 mmHg plus lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation (Sepsis-3, Box 3).
precipitants: Pneumonia; urinary or intra-abdominal infection; infected skin, tissue or vascular devices.
Recent hospitalisation, prior resistant isolates and recent broad-spectrum treatment change empirical choices (NCDC–ICMR, section 3.4; SSC 2026, section Multidrug resistance).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Cardiac dysfunction or congestion on bedside ultrasound; fluids may worsen pulmonary oedema. Assess alongside infection.
Bleeding or fluid loss with a compatible examination; investigate and treat the cause rather than assuming infection.
Acute unexplained hypoxaemia or right-heart strain; use the pulmonary embolism pathway if suspected.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Exposure and targeted testing redirect management; a positive result does not exclude bacterial co-infection.

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is infection-associated organ dysfunction; septic shock adds persistent circulatory and metabolic failure (Sepsis-3, Box 3). Supportive care uses the Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) 2026 update.
keyMechanisms: An uncontrolled host response to infection injures organs beyond the initial site (Sepsis-3, Box 3).
Vasodilation and altered microcirculation impair tissue perfusion; resuscitation must balance perfusion against fluid overload (SSC 2026, section Resuscitation).
A rise in Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of at least 2 supports infection-related organ dysfunction; it is not a prerequisite for treatment (Sepsis-3, Box 3).
Raised lactate needs clinical interpretation: it supports risk assessment but does not independently prove infection (SSC 2026, section Serial lactate).

clinicalScenario: Fictitious teaching case: an adult with fever and new confusion arrives hypotensive after recent antibiotic exposure. Assess infection likelihood, perfusion and an anatomical source while obtaining cultures; do not wait for a score or microbiology result to treat shock.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise, stabilise and classify infection likelihood
actions: Assess airway, breathing and circulation; provide monitored care and call the senior clinician. Record the recognition time.

Request intensive care unit (ICU) support for shock, impaired airway protection or worsening respiratory/organ failure. Do not wait for the SOFA calculation (SSC 2026, sections Fluid resuscitation and ICU admission).
Give appropriate antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour; obtain cultures without delaying therapy (SSC 2026, section Antibiotic initiation).
Investigate rapidly; if infection concern persists, administer antimicrobials within 3 hours of first suspicion (SSC 2026, section Antibiotic initiation).

branches.condition: Low likelihood of infection without shock
actions: Withhold antibiotics while continuing reassessment and investigating alternatives (SSC 2026, section Antibiotic initiation).

clinicalManagement.title: Restore perfusion with reassessment
actions: For sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or shock, SSC 2026 suggests at least 30 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid in the first 3 hours, individualised to clinical context. Prefer balanced crystalloid; reassess after each bolus and stop further boluses if congestion or lack of responsiveness develops (SSC 2026, sections Fluid resuscitation and Fluid type).
Use a passive-leg-raise or measured response to a fluid challenge where available, alongside capillary refill, lactate, mental state and urine output (SSC 2026, section Resuscitation).

Start noradrenaline for persistent hypotension; unstable shock may need vasopressors alongside fluids. Initial MAP target 65 mmHg; for adults ≥65 years, SSC 2026 suggests 60–65 mmHg, individualised by the critical-care clinician (SSC 2026, sections Fluid resuscitation and Mean arterial pressure).

Do not delay a necessary vasopressor solely to obtain central access. Use a local peripheral-vasopressor protocol with site surveillance until central access is established; the product-specific preparation and peripheral concentration require pharmacy confirmation (SSC 2026, section Vasopressor administration).

clinicalManagement.title: Choose one empirical branch and obtain source control
clinicalManagement.timeframe: With initial antibiotics; source control ideally within 6 hours
actions: Use the medication branch matching community sepsis without shock, undifferentiated septic shock, or hospital-acquired infection. Do not stack these antibiotic backbones. A localised infection uses its site-specific pathway (NCDC–ICMR, section 3.4).
Select additional resistant Gram-positive cover from documented risk and the local antibiogram; avoid routine broadening in a low-risk patient (SSC 2026, section Multidrug resistance).

Suspected obstruction, abscess, perforation, necrotising tissue or infected device requires an urgent procedural plan; aim for source control within 6 hours when indicated (SSC 2026, section Source control).

clinicalManagement.title: Review cultures, narrow treatment and set the stop date
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Daily; mandatory empirical review at 48 hours
actions: Check organism, susceptibility, source control, response and drug toxicity. Stop unnecessary components; negative cultures with improvement support de-escalation (NCDC–ICMR, section 3.4, p. 29; SSC 2026, section Antimicrobial therapy).

Proposed Marifa prescribing safeguard: the empirical antibiotic authorisation expires at the 48-hour review and must be actively renewed with a diagnosis, total-course duration and calendar stop date. This is a review/renewal cap, not an instruction to discontinue essential therapy in unstable sepsis and not an Indian national total-course maximum.
For a confirmed focus, apply its organism- and site-specific duration; count all effective treatment already given. Do not invent a blanket sepsis course length (NCDC–ICMR, section 3.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate refractory illness and plan recovery
actions: Escalate worsening lactate, mentation, oxygenation or vasopressor requirement immediately; reassess shock type, source control, drug exposure and resistant pathogens (SSC 2026, sections Resuscitation and Vasopressors).
For patients needing ICU admission, SSC 2026 suggests transfer within 6 hours. Use monitored transfer with an accepting team and a documented infusion plan.

Before discharge reconcile medicines, explain the infection and residual problems, and give a written treatment stop date and follow-up ownership (SSC 2026, sections Transitions of care and Hospital discharge).

guidelineComparison.title: Indian national baseline and current international supportive-care guidance

values: Section 3.4 pp. 30–31: 30 mL/kg rapidly for hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L.
Fluid resuscitation: at least 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours for hypoperfusion/shock, individualised with repeated reassessment.
Section 3.4 p. 29: undifferentiated community shock table includes a glycopeptide with the carbapenem.
Multidrug resistance: cover a resistant pathogen when risk is high; avoid routine coverage when risk is low. Risk-based branch selection needs local stewardship sign-off.
Section 3.4: source, organism and clinical course determine duration; de-escalation review at 48 hours.
No universal total-course maximum. Proposed Marifa 48-hour empirical authorisation expiry is a review safeguard, not a national treatment stop.
Mean arterial pressure: general initial target 65 mmHg; adults ≥65 years may start at 60–65 mmHg with clinical individualisation.

title: Acute bacterial meningitis (India)

symptoms: Fever, severe headache, neck discomfort, vomiting or photophobia (WHO 2025, section 1.5).
Confusion or unusual behaviour; older or immunocompromised adults may have an incomplete presentation.
physicalSigns: Neck stiffness, altered consciousness, focal neurological findings or seizures.
Look for a non-blanching rash and systemic shock; absence of a rash does not exclude meningococcal disease.
redFlags: Airway compromise, shock, new seizures, focal deficits or deteriorating consciousness require immediate senior/critical-care assessment.

Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) <10, focal signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilloedema, new adult seizures or severe immunocompromise: assess for cranial imaging before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, section A.4).
precipitants: Community respiratory pathogens; recent exposure to a meningococcal case.
Pregnancy, older age and immunocompromise change Listeria risk and empirical treatment. Recent neurosurgery or a shunt requires a separate healthcare-associated pathway (NCDC–ICMR sections 2.3–2.4).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: CSF often has lymphocytic predominance and preserved glucose, but an early result cannot safely exclude bacterial infection (WHO section A.2).
Prominent behavioural change, focal deficits or seizures; follow the India encephalitis pathway when the syndromes overlap (NCDC–ICMR section 2.2).
A longer constitutional illness and lymphocyte-predominant CSF suggest a different diagnostic and treatment pathway (NCDC–ICMR section 2.3).
Consider with severe immunocompromise; cryptococcal testing and opening pressure guide a distinct pathway. Routine bacterial-meningitis steroids are inappropriate (WHO section B.3).
Abrupt headache or a focal syndrome requires urgent imaging; do not perform an unsafe lumbar puncture (WHO section A.4).

pathophysiology.summary: Inflammation of the meninges can rapidly cause neurological injury and systemic illness; early pathogen-directed treatment and complication surveillance are essential (WHO 2025, sections 1.5 and B.1).
keyMechanisms: Inflammatory cells and protein enter the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) as the blood–brain barrier is disrupted (WHO 2025, section A.2).
Bacterial consumption and impaired transport contribute to low CSF glucose relative to blood (WHO 2025, section A.2).
Cerebral oedema, vascular complications and seizures can threaten consciousness and airway protection (WHO 2025, sections B.4 and B.6).
Antibiotics can reduce culture yield, so collect specimens promptly when safe without delaying treatment (WHO 2025, sections A.2 and B.2).

clinicalScenario: Fictitious teaching case: an adult presents with fever, headache and new confusion. Obtain blood cultures and decide whether lumbar puncture is safe while preparing immediate treatment. Imaging must not become a barrier to antibiotics.

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise, protect staff and prepare specimens
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediate; treatment within 1 hour of admission
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation and neurological status; call critical care for airway compromise, shock or ongoing seizures (WHO sections B.1, B.4 and B.6).

Take cultures and bloods while preparing antibiotics; initiate treatment as soon as possible and within 1 hour of admission. Do not wait for imaging or puncture results (NCDC–ICMR section 2.3; WHO toolkit, slide 33).
Use droplet precautions when meningococcal infection is suspected and involve infection control for the duration and contact assessment; do not improvise a prophylaxis regimen.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose the diagnostic route
actions: Perform lumbar puncture promptly when safe. Defer for cardiorespiratory instability, relevant bleeding risk or local puncture-site infection (WHO section A.1).

Where imaging is available, GCS <10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilloedema, new adult seizures or severe immunocompromise warrant imaging first. If imaging is unavailable, defer puncture while these risk features persist (WHO section A.4).
When puncture is delayed, blood cultures and treatment precede imaging. Send the CSF panel listed in Investigations once safe; retain a sample for additional tests (WHO sections A.2–A.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Select one empirical antibacterial pathway
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately after cultures when obtainable without delay
actions: Use ceftriaxone as the standard community-acquired backbone. Add vancomycin only when resistant pneumococci are a concern; check the local antibiogram (NCDC–ICMR section 2.3).
For Listeria risk, add ampicillin to the ceftriaxone pathway. Do not treat pregnancy as ordinary undifferentiated fever (NCDC–ICMR section 2.3; WHO section B.2.1).

The Indian table also gives a meropenem-plus-vancomycin alternative for immunocompromised adults or age >50 years. This replaces the ceftriaxone branch; it is not stacked on top. Discuss selection with infection specialists and document why broadening is required (NCDC–ICMR section 2.3).

Give eligible adjunctive dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose. Stop when bacterial infection is unlikely or the identified pathogen does not justify continuation; maximum 4 days. Do not use this steroid pathway for cryptococcal meningitis or cerebral malaria (WHO section B.3; WHO toolkit slides 31–32).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor complications and review microbiology
actions: Reassess consciousness, pupils, seizures, haemodynamics, oxygenation, fluid balance and renal function during the acute illness. Escalate any deterioration immediately; do not impose fluid restriction routinely (WHO sections B.4–B.6).

At the 48-hour review, document organism, susceptibility, narrowed treatment, effective treatment days and calendar stop date. If no organism is identified, explicitly select the national or WHO duration policy in the comparison table rather than blending them.

Persistent fever, new focal signs or lack of recovery require a diagnostic review for resistance, a collection, hydrocephalus or an alternative infection; do not simply extend the same regimen (WHO sections B.2 and B.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Apply a pathogen-specific stop and assess recovery
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before each planned course completion and discharge
actions: Indian default uncomplicated bacterial meningitis: 10–14 days, with a maximum routine plan of 14 days; confirmed meningococcus 5–7 days, Haemophilus influenzae 7–10 days and pneumococcus 10–14 days may use the WHO pathogen-specific plan after specialist review (NCDC–ICMR section 2.3; WHO Table 3.2).

Listeria: 21 days. Gram-negative bacilli or staphylococci require at least 21 days under the Indian guidance: no universal upper cap is established. Use specialist-prescribed stop dates and renewed authorisation; never truncate an indicated course to satisfy a software cap (NCDC–ICMR section 2.3).
Assess neurological and hearing sequelae before discharge. Arrange formal audiology before discharge or within 4 weeks, plus at least one clinical review within 4 weeks (WHO sections C.2 and C.4).

title: Acute undifferentiated fever (India)

symptoms: Fever with headache, chills, muscle or joint pain and malaise (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).

Floodwater or animal-urine exposure with compatible renal/hepatic or pulmonary illness; send targeted serology and escalate organ dysfunction.
Persistent compatible illness and a cultured organism support the diagnosis; use the existing India enteric-fever pathway.
Urine, chest, abdominal or device findings redirect to a source-specific pathway.
Medication reaction or inflammatory disease becomes more likely when repeated clinical assessment and targeted tests do not support infection.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute undifferentiated fever is a presenting syndrome, not a pathogen diagnosis. Early viral, bacterial, parasitic and non-infective illness can overlap; test selection depends on illness day, exposure and severity (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).
keyMechanisms: A systemic response can produce fever, headache and myalgia before a localising sign appears (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).
Malaria, dengue and rickettsial disease require different tests and treatment; an early negative assay may reflect timing rather than absence of infection (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).
Organ dysfunction or shock changes the problem from stable fever assessment to emergency resuscitation (NCDC–ICMR section 3.4).
Many uncomplicated febrile illnesses resolve without antibiotics; unnecessary exposure adds adverse effects and resistance selection (ICMR 2022, section Principles of empiric therapy).

clinicalScenario: Fictitious teaching case: a non-pregnant adult has persistent fever without an obvious focus after rural travel. First decide whether there is shock or organ dysfunction; only a stable patient enters the timed outpatient diagnostic pathway.

clinicalManagement.title: Triage severity before using the fever-day algorithm
actions: Check circulation, mental state, breathing and oral intake. Shock or organ dysfunction requires immediate hospital management, not observation until the next diagnostic day (NCDC–ICMR sections 3.1 and 3.4).
Record onset date, travel/residence, outbreak exposure, prior medicines, pregnancy possibility and immune state. Re-examine for a focal source.

clinicalManagement.title: Use supportive care for uncomplicated early illness
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Illness days 1–2, only if stable and without a high-risk condition
actions: National guidance permits deferring routine investigations and antimicrobials in uncomplicated early fever. Give oral fluids as tolerated and symptom relief when required; provide explicit return precautions (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).

Do not prescribe an antibiotic simply because fever is present. Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs when dengue/bleeding or renal injury is possible; choose the symptom-relief branch and reassess (ICMR acute fever principles; paracetamol product information).

clinicalManagement.title: Select tests by timing and exposure
actions: Days 3–4: blood count/differential, liver and renal tests, urine examination, glucose and targeted malaria/dengue testing (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).
After >5 days: add 2 blood-culture sets, selected IgM tests for dengue/chikungunya/scrub typhus/leptospirosis and chest X-ray (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).
After >7 days: reassess the entire differential and add abdominal ultrasound or directed tests. This is a trigger for reassessment, not permission to cycle antibiotics (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).
Investigate earlier with immunocompromise, pregnancy, worsening symptoms or a new localising sign. The India roadmap takes precedence over the older ICMR page where chest-imaging timing differs.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat a supported diagnosis; reserve empirical therapy
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After assessment; urgent treatment if instability develops
actions: Positive malaria/dengue tests or a localised syndrome redirect to the corresponding India pathway; do not continue the undifferentiated-fever regimen automatically.

Selected non-pregnant stable adults with credible rickettsial suspicion may receive doxycycline after specimens and malaria/dengue assessment. Review the need at 48 hours; an uncomplicated confirmed/strongly supported rickettsiosis uses a 7-day course, with the stop date written at initiation (ICMR 2022, Principles of empiric therapy and Rickettsial infections table).

Pregnancy, severe allergy or complicated rickettsial disease needs the appropriate specialist pathway. The short uncomplicated regimen does not cover encephalitis, shock or another established diagnosis.

clinicalManagement.title: Arrange reassessment and escalate deterioration
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Reassess within 48 hours; immediately for a red flag
actions: Review symptoms, examination, results and medicines within 48 hours; arrange earlier review if risk warrants. Contact the patient for actionable cultures rather than waiting for a planned visit (ICMR 2022, Principles of empiric therapy).

Admit or urgently refer if perfusion, breathing, mentation, bleeding, renal function or oral intake deteriorates. Persistent unresolved fever requires diagnostic review, not repeated empirical antibiotic courses.

patientEducation: Explain why a pathogen diagnosis may not be clear initially and why routine antibiotics can cause harm.
Return immediately with fainting, confusion, breathing difficulty, bleeding, reduced urine or inability to drink.
Explain which tests are pending, how results will be communicated and the medicine stop dates.
lifestyleAndDiet: Maintain oral fluids and food as tolerated; return if intake becomes inadequate.
Use mosquito protection and exposure-specific food/water precautions; avoid self-starting antibiotics or steroid combinations.
mdtReferrals: Emergency/critical care for instability or organ dysfunction.
Infectious diseases/microbiology for unresolved fever, positive cultures, complicated rickettsial illness or resistant organisms.
Obstetrics for pregnancy with systemic illness; public health/infection control for suspected clusters or notifiable disease under the relevant programme.
dischargeCriteria: Stable circulation, breathing and mental state; no organ dysfunction requiring admission.
Tolerating oral intake and medicines when prescribed.
A reliable review/result-contact plan is documented.
Patient understands the red flags and can reach urgent care if worse.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Reassess within 48 hours, including examination, results, antibiotic indication and stop date; earlier for any deterioration. Re-evaluate persistent fever with the timed national work-up rather than extending empirical antibiotics (ICMR 2022, Principles of empiric therapy; NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Acute fever without a clear focus after history and examination; severity and exposure determine investigation rather than a fixed antibiotic prescription (NCDC–ICMR section 3.1).
Shock or infection-associated organ dysfunction requires the sepsis or identified disease emergency pathway, regardless of the day of fever (NCDC–ICMR section 3.4).

A clinician may consider it after negative malaria/dengue rapid tests with persistent compatible illness; reserve this branch for a credible rickettsial suspicion and reassess at 48 hours (ICMR 2022, Principles of empiric therapy).

teaching.scope: Stable adult fever without a focus in India; high-risk and unstable presentations exit to an urgent disease-specific pathway.
learningObjectives: Triage severity before using illness-day testing.
Avoid routine antibiotics and document any selected course and review.
keyPoints: An early negative test may not exclude disease.
Severe illness overrides the stable day-based pathway.
pitfalls: Waiting for day 5 in a shocked or immunocompromised patient.
Cycling broad-spectrum antibiotics instead of repeating the assessment.
